title: Fetch vs. Form Page Reload
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: A p5.js comparison of two simulated robot controller pages. The form page reloads after every click and loses clicks made during the reload; the fetch() page only updates its status text. A timeline shows request time, blank-page time, robot start times, and missed clicks, while sliders change network delay and page size.

educational.topic: Asynchronous robot control with the JavaScript Fetch API
learningObjectives: Compare a form submission that reloads the whole page with a fetch() call that updates part of the page
Explain why clicks made during a page reload are lost
Explain how page size and network delay affect each approach
Explain why fetch() makes robot control smoother and safer
prerequisites: HTTP POST, HTML page generation, and the Fetch API from Chapter 11

controls.label: Page buttons (Forward, Back, Left, Right, Stop)
controls.purpose: Send a command from one simulated page

controls.label: Click both
controls.purpose: Press the chosen command on both pages at once

controls.label: Fast clicks
controls.purpose: Press Forward, Left, Stop, Forward within one second on both pages

equations: form: busy time per click = network delay + page size x 8 ms
fetch: time per click = network delay + about 5 ms for the status text
robot starts moving at click time + network delay / 2
assumptions: A click on the form page while it is loading is lost
fetch() requests are small (about 10 bytes), so page size does not matter
limitations: Does not model browser caching or HTTP keep-alive
The robot server is assumed fast enough to answer every request

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Side-by-side comparison with a controlled experiment
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Clickable simulated pages with a live timeline and parameter sliders
keyQuestions: What happens to a click made while the form page is reloading?
Why does page size matter for the form page but not for fetch()?
Which lines of sendCmd() run while the request is in flight?
Why is fetch() safer for a Stop button?
commonMisconceptions: fetch() makes the network faster (the request takes the same time; the page just does not reload)
The robot's server code must change to support fetch()
A page reload is instant, so it cannot cause problems
assessmentOpportunities: Table of reload time versus page size
Count of registered and missed clicks during Fast clicks
Exit ticket explaining an unreliable Stop button
